name: Loops and Functions
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: Steer loops with break and continue, and write functions with defaults, scope, lambdas and comprehensions.

lesson.intro: Loops repeat work, and functions package work under a name so you can reuse it. This lesson covers how to steer a loop, how values flow in and out of functions, where variables live, and two compact tools: lambdas and list comprehensions.

sections.title: Steering loops with break and continue
sections.body:
Inside a loop, `break` exits the loop immediately, and `continue` skips the rest of the current pass and moves on to the next item. Both affect only the innermost loop they are in.

`enumerate()` gives you the index and the item together, which is cleaner than keeping a counter yourself.

Don't add or remove items from a list while you loop over it. The loop tracks a position, so removing an item shifts the rest left and the loop skips one. Loop over a copy, or build a new list instead.

check.question: In the first loop, what would print if break were replaced with continue?
check.explanation: With continue, 0 is skipped instead of ending the loop, and the odd numbers 7 and 9 are skipped as well. The loop goes on to reach 2, so 4 and 2 print.

sections.title: Functions: return versus print
sections.body:
A function is defined with `def`, a name and a list of parameters. Calling it runs its body with the arguments you pass in.

`return` sends a value back to the caller and ends the function immediately, even in the middle of a loop. `print` only shows text on the screen; the caller gets nothing it can use.

A function that finishes without reaching a `return` returns None. A common bug is printing a result inside a function and then trying to use the function's value in a calculation.
sections.code:
def area(w, h):
    return w * h

def show_area(w, h):
    print(w * h)

a = area(3, 4)        # prints nothing; a is 12
b = show_area(3, 4)   # prints 12; b is None
print(a + 1)          # 13
print(b)              # None

check.question: Which statement about return is true?
choices: The lines after a return statement still run before the function ends
return ends the function and hands a value back to the caller
return prints its value on the screen
Every function must contain a return statement
check.explanation: Once return runs, the function stops and the caller receives the value. return doesn't print anything, and a function without return is allowed: it returns None.

sections.title: Parameters, defaults and flexible arguments
sections.body:
A parameter can have a default value that is used when the caller leaves that argument out, as in `def greet(name, greeting="Hello")`. Parameters with defaults must come after those without. Callers can also name arguments: `greet("Ben", greeting="Hi")`.

A default value is created once, when the `def` line runs, not on each call. If the default is mutable, such as a list, every call that uses the default shares that same list, and changes pile up between calls. Use None as the default and create the list inside the function.

`*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and `**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. The names are only conventions; the stars do the work.

check.question: Why is def f(items=[]) risky?
choices: Python forbids lists as default values
The list is copied on every call, which is slow
items is always None inside the function
The default list is created once and shared by every call that uses it
check.explanation: Defaults are evaluated once, when the function is defined. Every call that relies on the default appends to the same list, so values from earlier calls leak into later ones. Python allows it, which is why it is a trap rather than an error.

sections.title: Scope: where variables live
sections.body:
Variables created inside a function are local: they exist only while the function runs and are invisible outside it. Parameters are local too.

A function can read a global variable, one defined at the top level of the file. Python looks it up when the function runs, so it sees the current value.

But if a function assigns to a name anywhere in its body, Python treats that name as local for the whole function. The assignment creates a new local variable and leaves the global alone, and reading the name before the assignment raises UnboundLocalError.

The `global` keyword can override this, but passing values in as arguments and returning results keeps functions easier to test and understand.
sections.code:
count = 0

def bump():
    count = 10      # a new local variable
    return count

print(bump())   # 10
print(count)    # 0, the global is unchanged

def bump_broken():
    count += 1      # UnboundLocalError when called
    return count

check.question: A global variable total exists. A function runs total = 5 and returns. What happens to the global total?
choices: Nothing; the function created its own local total
check.explanation: Assignment inside a function creates a local variable unless the function declares global total. The global keeps its old value.

sections.title: Lambdas and list comprehensions
sections.body:
A lambda is a small unnamed function written as one expression: `lambda w: len(w)` takes w and returns its length. Lambdas are handy where a function is needed briefly, most often as the `key` for `sorted()`, `min()` or `max()`.

A list comprehension builds a list in one line: `[expression for item in iterable]`. Add `if condition` at the end to keep only some items. It reads like a sentence: "n times n, for each n in the range, if n is even".

Use a regular `def` or loop when the logic needs more than one simple expression.
sections.code:
words = ["pear", "fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w)))   # ['fig', 'pear', 'banana']

squares = [n * n for n in range(5)]
print(squares)                     # [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

even_squares = [n * n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0]
print(even_squares)                # [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]

check.question: What does [c.upper() for c in "abc"] produce?
check.explanation: Square brackets make a list comprehension, which always builds a list, not a tuple. It loops over each character and uppercases it, giving three items, and it doesn't join them into one string.

keyTerms.definition: Skips the rest of the current loop pass and moves on to the next item.
The value a function hands back to its caller; None if no return runs.
A parameter with a value used when the caller omits it; the value is created once, at definition.
The names created inside a function, visible only while that function runs.
Parameters that collect extra positional arguments into a tuple and extra keyword arguments into a dict.
A small anonymous function made of a single expression.
A compact expression that builds a list from an iterable, optionally filtering items.

summary: break leaves the innermost loop, and continue jumps to its next pass.
return hands a value back and ends the function; print only displays text.
Default values are created once, so use None instead of a mutable default.
Assigning to a name inside a function makes that name local to the function.
Lambdas suit short key functions, and comprehensions turn a loop that builds a list into one line.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 3 (3 and 6) are skipped by continue. 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 are added, giving 19. When n reaches 8, break ends the loop, so 8 and 9 are never added.

questions.question: How many lines does this print?
questions.explanation: break only exits the inner loop. For each i, the inner loop prints i and 0, then breaks when j is 1, and the outer loop carries on. That gives three lines, not one.
questions.concept: break exits only the innermost loop

questions.question: Complete the loop so it prints a and b and skips the empty string.
questions.explanation: continue skips the print for the empty string and moves on to b. break would end the loop before b, and pass does nothing, so an empty line would print. return is only valid inside a function.

questions.question: This should remove every even number, but it prints [4, 5]. Why?
choices: Removing items from the list being looped over shifts the rest, so some are skipped; loop over a copy such as nums[:]
remove() deletes items by index, not by value
n % 2 == 0 is true for odd numbers
The for loop runs only once, because nums changes length
questions.explanation: After 2 is removed, 4 shifts into position 0, but the loop moves on to position 1, which now holds 5, so 4 is never checked. Looping over nums[:] avoids this, or build a new list with [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 1].
questions.concept: changing a list while looping over it

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
def double(n):
    print(n * 2)

result = double(5)
print(result)
questions.explanation: Calling double(5) prints 10. The function has no return, so result is None, and the second print shows None. To use the value later, return n * 2 instead of printing it.
questions.concept: a function without return gives None

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: return ends the function the moment it runs, even in the middle of a loop. 3 and 7 are skipped, 8 is returned, and 10 is never checked. return -1 only runs if the loop finishes without finding an even number.

questions.question: Why does this crash with a TypeError?
questions.code:
def average(nums):
    total = sum(nums)
    avg = total / len(nums)

score = average([80, 90])
print(score + 5)
choices: sum() can't add a list of ints
average computes avg but never returns it, so score is None and None + 5 fails
avg is a float, and floats can't be added to ints
len(nums) is 0, so the division fails
questions.explanation: Without return avg, the function returns None, and the error comes from score + 5 outside the function. Floats and ints add fine, and the list has two items, so the division works.

questions.question: What is the difference between returning a value and printing it?
questions.answer: print shows text on the screen and gives the caller nothing back (the function returns None). return hands a value back to the caller, which can store it or use it in more calculations. A function can print without returning and return without printing.
questions.explanation: Mixing these up is the most common reason a function's result turns out to be None.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: history=[] is created once, when def runs. All three calls append to that same list, so the third call sees three items. Each call does not get a fresh empty list.

questions.question: Complete the check so each call without a history argument gets a fresh list.
questions.explanation: None is the placeholder default, so test for it with is None and create the list inside the function. history is [] is always False, because [] builds a new list each time, so the list is never created and append fails.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: *args gathers the positional arguments into a tuple, which prints with parentheses. **kwargs gathers the keyword arguments into a dict. Because the function has **kwargs, the keyword unit is accepted instead of raising TypeError.

questions.question: Python refuses to run this file at all. Why?
choices: f-strings can't be returned from a function
greet must be called with positional arguments
A parameter without a default can't follow one with a default; put name first
questions.explanation: This is a SyntaxError, found before anything runs. Parameters without defaults must come before those with defaults: def greet(name, greeting="Hi"). Calling with a keyword argument is fine once the definition is fixed.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
x = 5

def change():
    x = 99
    return x

change()
print(x)
questions.explanation: x = 99 inside change() creates a local variable, so the global x is never touched and still holds 5. change() did return 99, but nothing stored it.
questions.concept: assignment inside a function is local

questions.question: Calling increment() raises UnboundLocalError. Why?
questions.code:
counter = 0

def increment():
    counter = counter + 1
    return counter

increment()
choices: Assigning to counter inside the function makes it local, so reading it on the right side fails before it has a value
counter must be declared with a type first
Functions can never read variables defined outside them
questions.explanation: Because the function assigns to counter, Python treats counter as local throughout the function, and counter + 1 reads that local before it is set. Functions can read globals as long as they don't also assign to them. A cleaner design takes counter as a parameter and returns counter + 1.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
rate = 2

def scale(n):
    return n * rate

rate = 3
print(scale(5))
questions.explanation: scale() never assigns to rate, so rate refers to the global, and Python looks it up when the function is called, not when it is defined. By the time of the call rate is 3, so the result is 5 * 3 = 15.
questions.concept: globals are read at call time

questions.question: Complete the call so the pairs are sorted by their number.
questions.explanation: key needs a function that takes one item and returns the value to sort by, and lambda p: p[1] returns each pair's number. lambda p: p[0] sorts by letter. lambda: p[1] takes no parameter, so sort raises TypeError, and a bare p[1] raises NameError because p doesn't exist.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code: print([n * 2 for n in range(6) if n % 3 == 0])
questions.explanation: range(6) gives 0 to 5. The filter keeps numbers divisible by 3, which are 0 and 3, and each kept number is doubled, giving [0, 6].
